title: Searching Better
segs: Chapter 23. Searching Better.

A complaint arrived on a Monday. Farah Sheikh forwarded it without comment, which was how Anaya knew it mattered. A customer in Nashik had asked the chatbot what the late fee on her electricity bill was, and it had said one hundred rupees. She had paid three days after the due date, and Sahaj had charged her one hundred and fifty.
She wasn’t very angry, and her message was polite. She simply wanted to know why a machine speaking for the company had said one thing while the company did another.

Within the hour, Lakshmi Iyer arrived at the glass room with a printout and a face from which all expression had been carefully removed. She asked which figure was right. Imran Qureshi checked and said one hundred and fifty, because the fee had gone up in January. She asked where the machine had found a hundred.
The case: the fee that used to be true.

The explanation took Imran twenty minutes to find, and it was ordinary. When the late-fee policy changed in January, someone had uploaded the new version to the folder the chatbot read from. Nobody had removed the old one.

So both versions sat in the store, cut into chunks, each with its own embedding. When the customer asked her question, the search found the two chunks about the late fee. They were nearly identical except for the figure, and the old one happened to score slightly higher. It went to the model, and the model wrote a fluent, confident, grounded answer from last year’s rule.
Everything had worked. The search found the right topic. The model used what it was given. The answer was grounded in a real document. The document was simply out of date.
Key idea: Relevance is not correctness.

Better ranking would not have helped. Last year’s policy is about late fees, and it matches the question as well as this year’s does. Relevance and correctness are different questions, and nothing in the search knew the difference.
Four improvements.

The work of the previous month gave the team a calm way to look at this. They had an answer key for the chatbot’s search: ten questions in the customers’ own words, with a first score of six out of ten. Imran took four techniques in turn and measured each one against the same ten.

Table 23.1: Four improvements to search, measured on the same ten questions. Hybrid search. What it does: Runs keyword search and search by meaning together, and combines the two lists, so there is no longer a choice to make. "Clause 14.2" came from one and "paisa kab milega" from the other. Score: 6 to 7. Reranking. What it does: Fetches the best fifty pieces cheaply, then has a slower, more careful model read the question and each piece together and put the best few on top. It improves recall and precision at once, at the price of extra time and a second call, which is why it runs on fifty pieces and not on the whole library. Score: 7 to 8. Contextual retrieval. What it does: Before storing each chunk, a model writes one sentence saying where the chunk sits in its document ("This is from the refund section of the Late Payment Policy, about overpayments"), and the sentence is stored with it. A piece that began "the aforesaid amount" now carries a note on what the amount is. Score: 8 to 9. Metadata filtering. What it does: Each chunk is labelled with its document, its version, the dates between which it is in force and who may see it. Before the search scores anything, any chunk that is not current is thrown out. Score: No change.
The fourth technique is the one that didn’t move the score. The labels are called metadata, and throwing out chunks by those labels before any scoring is metadata filtering.
The question nobody had asked.
Anaya worked out why the score hadn’t moved. The answer key didn’t contain the question. None of the ten asked about anything that had changed.

So Imran added it as row eleven: what is the late fee on an electricity bill? The correct answer was one hundred and fifty rupees. Without the filter, the system answered a hundred. With the filter on, it answered a hundred and fifty. He ran it a hundred times to be sure, and the result was the same every time.
Key idea: The only technique that guarantees something.

Hybrid search makes the right chunk more likely to come up. Reranking makes it more likely to be on top. The extra sentence makes it more likely to be understood. No ranking technique can stop a repealed policy from outranking the current one, because ranking is about relevance and this is about correctness. A filter acts before the scoring. It doesn’t make the wrong thing less likely. It makes it impossible.

Anaya recognised a distinction she had begun to look for in everything. One kind of method makes a failure rarer. Another kind removes its cause. She wrote "row eleven" on the whiteboard in black, below the old red line. It was the first row of the answer key that had come from a customer.
What the labels are for.
Lakshmi had stayed. She asked what else was on the labels. Imran listed them: the document, the version, the dates it applies, and who is allowed to see it.

Lakshmi repeated the last item. There were internal documents in the folder, such as the collections playbook and the staff handbook. What would have happened before, she asked, if a customer’s question had matched the handbook? Imran said the search would have found the handbook. She asked him to show how that was now prevented. A filter before the search, he said. A customer’s request can see only the chunks labelled for customers.

She nodded with an expression Anaya hadn’t seen on her before. It wasn’t quite approval. It was the look of someone who has found a firm floor. For the first time, a tool in the building was doing what Lakshmi had asked of every system for twenty years: making the wrong thing impossible instead of unlikely.

Anaya saw that the same idea belonged in the guard. Every message arrives from a place: the order-tracking screen, the loan-status screen, the free chat. An identity number typed into a screen built to collect one may be exactly right. The same number in the free chat is not.

If the rule-keeper knows where a message came from before it decides anything, it can apply different rules without any clever step. The purpose of a message was just another label, and an honest one. She added a column to the specification.
One more idea, set aside.

One more technique remained. Imran described it and then put it off. A model can be allowed to run several searches itself, read the results and rewrite its question, using the loop from Chapter 20. This is agentic search.

It can find better evidence. But it multiplies the cost in the way that chapter showed, and it brings the same risks. He wrote it on the board under "later", a column that had begun to look like a good place for a number of things.
Chapter summary.
Plain search can be improved in four ways, and each is worth measuring against the same answer key.

Hybrid search runs keyword and meaning search together, so no choice has to be made between them. Reranking fetches many candidates, then has a slower model reread and reorder them. It improves both what is found and how clean it is, at some cost in time. Contextual retrieval attaches to each chunk a sentence about where it comes from, and repairs orphans. Metadata filtering labels chunks with version, dates and audience, and filters on those labels before any scoring. It is the only technique here that can promise a result, because relevance and correctness are different questions. Agentic search lets a model search repeatedly, and it multiplies the cost.
A good answer key grows from real failures, and the best new row is the one a customer wrote.
Next, you’ll meet a much nastier problem, in which the text a model reads starts giving it orders.
